name: Eight Questions Before the Board Approves an AI Contract
title: Eight Questions Before the Board Approves an AI Contract
answer: Before a school board approves any AI contract, it should require written answers to eight practical questions that make the risks visible before money is spent. Approval should also not be the end of oversight: an annual review keeps the board informed about which tools are in use, what they produced, what incidents occurred, and what they cost. This matters because a district can otherwise commit large sums to a tool that is later shut down, as happened with the Los Angeles chatbot.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: This idea is a set of eight questions a board member can ask about any AI proposal, none of which requires technical knowledge. It exists because boards approve contracts, and AI contracts carry risks that ordinary purchasing questions may not surface. The text points to the Los Angeles chatbot, which went from launch to shutdown within months after the district had paid about $3 million. Better questions at the start would not have prevented every problem, but they would have made the risks visible before the money was spent. Each question should have a clear written answer before the vote, and if staff cannot answer them, the proposal is not ready and should be sent back for more work.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, the eight questions become a written checklist that staff must complete before the board votes on an AI proposal. The text does not give grade bands for this idea, because it is a governance practice rather than a classroom one. If staff cannot provide clear answers in writing, the board sends the proposal back for more work instead of approving it. Approval is not the last time the board sees the tool: each spring the superintendent brings an annual AI review covering which tools are in use, what results they produced, what incidents were reported, and what they cost. That yearly report turns the eight questions into a repeating cycle rather than a single vote, and tools that cannot show results by the second review deserve a hard look, with some stopped.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers a concrete case rather than a formal study. It states that the Los Angeles chatbot moved from launch to shutdown in a matter of months, and that the district had paid about $3 million by then, citing EdSurge, 2024. The book's own claim is measured: better questions at the start would not have prevented every problem, but they would have made the risks visible before the money was spent. No other study, figure, or finding is given for the eight questions themselves. The evidence label in the text is a cited news report, not research on the questions as a method.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set out plainly. The eight questions do not require technical knowledge, but they do require clear answers in writing before the vote, and a proposal without them is not ready. The board keeps the decision: it can send a proposal back for more work, and it should not treat approval as the final word. The annual review is a required cycle, and tools that cannot show results by the second review deserve a hard look, with some stopped. The text does not claim the questions prevent every problem, only that they make risks visible before money is spent. Nothing here is legal advice; it describes a practice for board oversight.
